nodes.text: Portions of this article first appeared in the pages of Film Fantastic Quarterly, Cinemagic, and Shrunk!
I met Oscar Stutgart twenty-six years ago.

His involvement in film production for the better part of his forty-nine years had graced the industry with some of the most intricate and recognizable of classic film's miniature model work and tableaux design.

It was at the request of Heritage Pictures, involved in a puff piece commissioned under the auspice of then-humbled film financier Ben Goddard, that I was flown out to visit Oscar's recommissioned aircraft hanger production office, tucked a few miles from the Pacific Ocean, hidden amidst the quiet, oddly out of time cheesemaking town of Tillamook, Oregon.

Oscar, had he retired, would have done so about the time of my visit. He had one assistant, a local boy named Robert who couldn't afford to go to film school, and had served his early career in a purgatory indefinitely interned with Oscar.

It was heavily fogged when Robert met me at local diner Marley's, the sound of the waves just out of sight filled the small city street. I followed his car along a winding riverlet to the site of the production office.

Robert explained that Oscar supplemented his model construction with self-guided tours of old railway cars and aircraft that resided on the front side of the studio. It was retirees with cameras and young soldiers on leave who wandered the grounds as Robert led us into the plain-facade rear of the edifice.
An empty reception desk was stacked with old newspapers and film journals, which Robert said he hadn't gotten around to cataloging yet, movie posters rolled up in cardboard tubes stacked in a corner.
I was showed into a workroom, ill lit and crammed with miniature precision instruments and half-finished works in progress. Robert knocked on what looked like a closet door, and Oscar emerged.

He was close to seventy, skin heavily discolored and thickly bespeckled with many shoe stringed pairs of eyeglasses around his neck. His hands were scarred and mercury stained, his fingernails clipped so far as to become a tiny thick horn halfway down the tip of his finger.
He coughed once or twice while introducing himself, and asked about the film, and my coverage of it. He seemed to be in the dark about the production, aside from his own post-production contribution.
He explained to me how he never really liked the stories, so much as the spectacle, and even then, being as close to it as he was, he couldn't really be bothered.
jay rose was the first of us to disappear. These are the comics he contributed to the Small Wood Senior High newspaper.
